en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Śakra,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmabhadra, Imperially Appointed Court Honorable and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, under Imperial Edict.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Vipula, in the Śakra Cave, within the Amla Garden to the east of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, north of the village of Mahābrāhmaṇa, together with a great assembly.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard that the Buddha was staying at Mount Vaidehī in the Śakra Cave in the Magadha country, addressed the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, saying: "Do you know this?"

"I have heard that the Buddha is staying at Mount Vaidehī, on the Śakra Cave in the kingdom of Magadha; I wish to go together with you to the Buddha’s dwelling to attend upon and make offerings to him."
At that time, having heard these words, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha addressed Śakra,
saying: "Excellent,
O Lord of Devas!"
Having spoken these words, he took up his lute adorned with lapis lazuli gems and followed Śakra.

At that time, when the host of devas heard that Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha had resolved to go to the Buddha’s abode to attend upon and make offerings to him, they likewise each resolved their minds, desiring to follow and go to the Buddha’s abode to attend upon and make offerings to him.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha and his celestial host, vanished from that heaven and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, arrived at the side of Mount Vaidehaka in the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, a great light suddenly appeared on that mountain, illuminating it everywhere.
All the people living on the four sides of the mountain, having seen that light, said to one another:
"For what reason is there a great fire burning on this mountain, such that its original appearance is eclipsed and it resembles a mountain of jewels?"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha:
"Do you see this mountain possessing such exquisite and wondrous colors?"
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells therein, pure in the four requisites.

Furthermore, all the halls and palaces on this mountain are composed entirely of jewels; those who reside there have exhausted all afflictions and fully realized the fruits of sainthood, and even the gods of great power constantly abide here.
He spoke again, saying:
"Therefore, we find it difficult to encounter and meet such an opportunity; as previously stated regarding drawing near and making offerings, now is precisely the right time."
"You, Prince Pañcaśikha, Gandharva, should perform an offering with the musical instruments you carry.
Why is this? Because after this moment has passed, it will truly be difficult to encounter such an opportunity again."
At that time, having heard these words, the Gandharva prince addressed Śakra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Having spoken these words, he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess the supernormal power of the divine ear; there is nothing too far or too near that they cannot hear.

Having formed this thought, the *vīṇā* adorned with lapis lazuli jewels that he held began to vibrate, and from its sound there issued forth a verse (*gāthā*), wherein he spoke of his aspirations. That verse said:
“O noble lady Sūryaprabhā, you should request of your father the king that he grant me as your companion; this shall prove your virtue.
I am filled with longing for you, just as one tormented by heat longs for coolness.”
Longing for coolness, like a thirsty person yearning for water;
like a sick person longing for medicine, or a hungry person thinking of food;
like a great elephant caught by a hook, unable to move forward.
Just as an Arhat seeks the dharma of tranquil extinction, so too is the meaning of my present aspiration.
Greed and desire increase affliction; herein there is no reality whatsoever.
Failing to achieve their desired aims, they undergo various kinds of suffering.
May the fruit and reward obtained from the meritorious deeds I have performed— offering sustenance to the Arhats— be shared with you.
"I seek the daughter of the Sun; this resolve of mine is most firm.
O Śakra, Lord of the Devas, you should grant my wish.

At that time, the World-Honored One, from within the Śakra Cave, heard her voice from afar with his divine ear-penetration (divya-śrotra-abhijñā) and immediately used his supernormal power (ṛddhi-bala) to address the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha from a distance:
“Excellent! Excellent! Gandharva Prince, you are skilled in music!”
When the strings were struck, they produced a subtle and wondrous sound like the voice of a master singer, and when the song was sung, it again resembled the sound of the strings.
For what reason did this music continue for so long, and from within those strings did these verses emerge?
Furthermore, it is said that three kinds of voices are spoken in these verses: the voice of delight, the voice of a nāga, and the voice of an arhat.
At that time, the gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, heard the Buddha’s words from afar and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I recall that once there was a gandharva king named Drumala; that king had a daughter named Sūryaprabhā, whom my heart desired as a consort.

At that time, although I employed various skillful means, my wish was still not fulfilled; I then produced such music before the girl, and from the strings of the music there issued forth a verse, within which three kinds of sounds were spoken.
“World-Honored One!
When I play this music, the various hosts of devas in that Hall of Good Dharma will say to one another:

‘This prince of the gandharvas, Pañcaśikha, has neither seen nor heard our Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is endowed with the ten titles: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.’”
Thereupon, I said to the assembly of devas:
"You devas have well praised the virtues of the Buddha. The devas replied:
"O Pañcaśikha, Prince of the Gandharvas!
All the merits we have praised in the Buddha, we share with you.
Upon hearing the words of the devas, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha suddenly attained realization and replied:
"O Virtuous One! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
It was for this reason that I offered such music to the Buddha.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"Now this Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha’s roots and conditions have matured; even before reaching the Buddha, he has already extended his offerings."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, saying:
"Take my words and go to where the Buddha is; prostrate yourself at his feet and speak these words on my behalf:

'The Lord of Devas, Śakra, bows his head at your feet and inquires after the World-Honored One’s health—whether you are free from illness and affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, and whether your strength is secure.'"
"Are you free from any distress in your coming and going?
We, together with the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, now wish to come to the Buddha to approach him and make offerings.
Please grant us leave to do so."
At that time, having heard these words, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha addressed Śakra,
saying: “Excellent,
O Lord of Devas!”
Having spoken these words, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, has sent me here to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet and to inquire after the World-Honored One: Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and well-being secure?”
"Is there no distress in your coming and going?
We wish today to go to the Buddha's dwelling to attend upon and make offerings to him; therefore, we have sent you to hear the Buddha's instructions.
The Buddha then replied:
"You may return and inform Śakra and the assembly of devas that now is the very time.
Having received the Buddha’s holy command, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha returned to Śakra’s abode and delivered the World-Honored One’s words: "Now is the very time."
At that time, Śakra and the host of the Trāyastriṃśa devas went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and stood to one side.
Then, the Lord of Devas had this thought:
"This Śakravana Cave is narrow and cramped; how shall these countless celestial hosts sit?"

The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, immediately employed his supernatural powers to cause the cliff to expand in width, so that the assembly of devas could each find space without hindering one another.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and his celestial host each paid homage to the Buddha and sat down in order.
When the assembly had taken their seats, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
For a long night, I have delighted in desiring to see the Buddha and have delighted in hearing the True Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
I recall that at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, having entered the fire-element samādhi.

At that time, I was in the palace of Vaiśravaṇa, where I saw a lady named Subāhu among the women of that palace; seeing the Buddha enter this fire-element samādhi, she joined her palms in reverence and focused her mind single-mindedly on recollecting the Buddha.”
While I saw that the World-Honored One had not yet emerged from samādhi, I said to Subāhu:

"Wait until the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emerges from samādhi, and convey my sincere greetings to him, asking whether he has little illness and little affliction, whether his daily life is light and easy, and whether his strength is at peace."
"Is there no distress in your coming and going? He further said:
"Wait for the Buddha to emerge from his meditative concentration and convey my utmost sincerity, lest it be forgotten."
"World-Honored One!
Is this fact truly so?
The Buddha said:
“Śakra! This is indeed so.
That lady once offered you her respects and inquiries on my behalf.”
The Buddha spoke again:
"Lord of Devas!
While I was in samādhi, I also heard your words; not long thereafter, I emerged from samādhi."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In the past, I have heard that there are Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who appear in the world to perform great benefit, guiding beings according to their various types through great skillful means—sometimes concealing human form, and sometimes manifesting as celestial bodies."

I now know for myself that the Buddha has appeared in the world to bring great benefit, guiding beings according to their capacities through skillful means, sometimes remaining hidden and sometimes manifesting.
World-Honored One!

All the śrāvakas who left the household life to practice the holy life under the Buddha were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after their deaths; those devas delight in three things: namely, lifespan, physical appearance, and reputation.
“World-Honored One!

In the past, there was a Śākya girl named Guhyadattā who left the household life under the Buddha and maintained the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). She was constantly weary of the female body and sought the marks of a male. After her life ended, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as my son, named Guhyadatta; he possesses great majesty and power and is a true Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).”
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, there were three bhikṣus who practiced the path of the śrāvakas, yet they were unable to sever their hearts of greedy desire. After their lives ended, they were reborn in the heavenly realms as sons of the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, and constantly came to serve the Devaputra Guhyaka.”
At that time, the goddess Guhyadattā addressed the Gandharva son Vinata with these verses:
"In the past, I was a woman named Guhyadattā, possessed of wisdom;
weary of the female form, I sought the marks of a male and constantly made offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
At that time, I saw your three sons practicing the path of the śrāvakas;
born now into a lowly clan, they serve as my attendants.
You should know this now: I shall speak the truth to you.
When you were formerly a human being, you were fully provided with the four requisites;
yet you did not rely upon the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts. Now you should harbor shame and remorse.
To realize the mind is itself the True Dharma—only the wise are able to realize this.
In the past, we practiced together; drawing near to the Buddha, we heard the True Dharma.
We gave rise to faith and upheld the Buddha’s precepts, as well as making offerings to the noble assembly.
Because I practiced such right conduct, I have become a son of Śakra.
Possessing the great majesty of a deva, you know yourself as one of secret practice;
dwelling in a most excellent palace, you have transformed your female form into male.
You, son of a gandharva, have followed the Buddha to uphold the holy life.
Having heard the Buddha’s supreme Dharma, I have become his attendant.
Within the celestial realms, I have never before seen such service as I see now;
though I practiced the conduct of a śrāvaka, I was born into a lowly family.
"You, sons of gandharvas, have received my secret transformative teaching;
the births you have taken were not those of the sons of the Buddhas.
The sons of the gandharvas said:
"What the deva has spoken is true.
Because of our greed and desire, we have fallen into the realm of the gandharvas.
We now arouse diligence and contemplate only the Buddha’s True Dharma."
Knowing that desire gives rise to faults, one should sever that desirous mind.
Desire is a bond of affliction; its power surpasses the armies of Māra.
Because they abandon the Buddha’s true Dharma, they are not reborn in the superior heavens.
Śakra and Brahmā, seated in the assembly of the Good Dharma,
observed the sublime conduct of the gods who traverse the celestial realms.
Seeing me born into a lowly clan yet traversing the celestial realms, they were moved.
"Because my conduct was not upright, I have not attained the supreme fruit.
At that time, the deity Guhyapracāra addressed his father, Śakra, saying:
"Father King, you should now know: our Buddha is the Most Honored One."
Appearing in the world, he who has successfully subdued all the hosts of Māra is named Śākyamuni.
He is the son of that Buddha, yet he has lost his right mindfulness.
They fall into the realm of the gandharvas;
only one lacks correct awareness, while the other two return to the right path,
constantly inclining toward the Buddha’s bodhi and practicing the true Dharma.
Among all the śrāvakas seen here, there is none who can equal them.
Having distanced themselves from desires and being able to sever the afflictions,
they think only of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and no longer give rise to other thoughts.
"All dharmas not yet fully understood, those two shall correctly know;
they shall obtain the supreme fruit and be born in the Brahma Heaven.
"World-Honored One!"

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Devaputra Guhyacārin, I had certain matters regarding this that remained undecided; therefore, I have come to the presence of the Buddha, wishing to pose my questions.
“May the Buddha, out of compassion, graciously explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

“The Lord Śakra has, throughout the long night, been untiring, unremitting, free from dust, and free from defilement. What he asks is truly out of ignorance and not an act of Māra; I shall explain what he asks.”
Having formed this thought, he immediately spoke a verse, addressing Śakra:
"Śakra, you should now know: whatever meaning you desire to ask about according to what is pleasing in your mind, you should question me and I shall explain it for you."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke these verses and addressed the World-Honored One:
“Now that I have received the Buddha’s permission, I shall now make this request according to my own desire; may the Buddha graciously proclaim it for me.”
After Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For all devas, asuras, gandharvas, and ordinary beings, what constitutes their afflictions?”
The Buddha said,
"Affliction consists of hatred and attachment,
O Lord of the Devas, Śakra!"
All the devas, asuras, gandharvas, and even all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) thought to themselves:

"Alas! I have never previously harmed others, nor have I been resentful or unjust toward them; I have not fought, disputed, sued, litigated, or held a grudge against anyone. Why, then, do they act in such a manner toward me?"
"O Lord of Devas!
Such matters arise from hatred and attachment; because hatred and attachment arise, afflictions consequently come into being. Śakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so, just as the Buddha has taught. Now, having understood this meaning from the Buddha, I realize that hatred and attachment are the afflictions.”
"Having severed all doubt, your heart's desire shall be fulfilled.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, received it with joy and faith, and further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding these afflictions of aversion and attachment: what is their cause? What is their origin?
From what do they arise? What is their condition?
By what cause do they come to exist?
“For what reason does one attain non-existence?
The Buddha said,
“Lord of Devas!”

These afflictions of hatred and attachment have enemies and kin as their cause, arise from enemies and kin, are born from enemies and kin, and take enemies and kin as their condition; because of enemies and kin, there are the afflictions of hatred and attachment. If there were no enemies and kin, hatred and attachment would not exist.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as the Buddha has taught.

I have now understood this meaning from the Buddha: hatred and affection arise with afflictions as their cause, and with enemies and kin as their condition; if there were no enemies or kin, there would be no hatred or affection.”
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what cause do enemies and kin exist?"
From what do they accumulate?
By what are they produced?
Upon what conditions do they depend?
"By what cause does it exist?
By what cause does it not exist?
The Buddha told Śakra:

"Desire is the cause; from desire it arises, by desire it is born, with desire as its condition. Because of desire, there are enemies and kin; if there were no desire, enemies and kin would not exist."
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is just as the Buddha has said—that those who are enemies or kin exist because of desire.”
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From what cause does this desire arise?"
From what do they accumulate?
From what do they arise?
Upon what conditions do they depend?
"By what cause does it exist?
By what cause does it not exist?
The Buddha said:

“Śakra! What is desired exists because of doubt, arises from the accumulation of doubt, is produced by doubt, and has doubt as its condition. Because of doubt, there is what is desired; if there were no doubt, there would be no desire.”
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
So it is, so it is; as the Buddha has taught, that which is desired arises from doubt."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the cause of doubt?"
From what do they arise?
From what are they produced?
What is their condition?
"And by what cause does this doubt arise?
By what cause does it cease?
The Buddha told Śakra:

"Taking falsehood as the cause, arising from falsehood, born of falsehood, and conditioned by falsehood, because of falsehood there is doubt; because of doubt there arises desire; because of that desire there are enemies and kin; because of those enemies and kin there arise hatred and affection; because of hatred and affection, there come to be the wielding of swords and staves, litigation, and strife; the mind gives rise to flattery and crookedness, and speech is not truthful. From such various unwholesome dharmas of sinful karma, this great mass of suffering is accumulated."
"Lord of Devas!
If there is no falsehood, there is no doubt; if there is no doubt, there is no desire. When desire is absent, how could there be enmity or affection?"

When neither enemy nor kin is established, hatred and attachment naturally cease. Because hatred and attachment are absent, such various karmic offenses and unwholesome dharmas as brandishing swords and staves, litigation, strife, and contention, as well as deceitful intentions and false speech, are all completely extinguished. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering is extinguished.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, so it is; as the Buddha has said, because of doubt there is falsehood.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One!
By what dharma are illusory dharmas extinguished?
Furthermore, how should a bhikṣu practice?”
The Buddha told the Lord of Devas:
"That which extinguishes the false and illusory is called the Eightfold Noble Path.

The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; through these eight factors, the false and illusory are extinguished."
"If any bhikṣus practice this Dharma, they are said to be practicing the cessation of false delusions.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying, "So it is, so it is."
“World-Honored One!
That which extinguishes delusion is the Eightfold Noble Path.
Śakra then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the elimination of false dharmas, if a bhikṣu practices them, how many kinds of dharmas are there within the Prātimokṣa?
The Buddha said:
“Lord of Devas!
Regarding false dharmas, there are six kinds of dharmas within the Prātimokṣa. What are these six?
That is to say: the eye perceives forms, the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue discerns tastes, the body feels tangibles, and the mind discriminates phenomena.
Lord of Devas!
The eye’s observation of forms has two meanings: namely, that which is observable and that which is unobservable.
The unobservable refers to that which cannot be observed within the spheres of all defiled phenomena;
the observable refers to that which can be examined within the spheres of all wholesome phenomena.
"In this same way, from the eye observing visual objects, up to the mind discriminating mental phenomena, it is likewise so.
"World-Honored One!

I have now understood this meaning from the Buddha: that which is not to be observed consists of all unwholesome dharmas within the domain of the eye; if one were to observe them, it would increase defiled dharmas and diminish wholesome dharmas."
That which is worthy of contemplation consists of all wholesome phenomena within the domain of the eye; if one contemplates them, it serves to increase wholesome dharmas and diminish defiled dharmas.
Even so it is with the mental discrimination of dharmas.
World-Honored One!
Having now heard this Dharma from the Buddha, my aspirations and joys are fulfilled, and my doubts and perplexities are severed.
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu wishes to extinguish falsehood, how many dharmas should he sever?"
"How many dharmas should one practice?
The Buddha said,
"Lord of Devas!"
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to extinguish false dharmas, he should sever three things and practice three things:
first, doubt; second, longing; and third, meaningless speech.
Regarding these three kinds of dharmas, there are those that may be practiced and those that may not be practiced.

Those that should not be practiced refer to these three kinds of unwholesome dharmas, which one ought to sever and not perform; if one were to practice them, they would increase unwholesome dharmas and diminish wholesome dharmas.

Those that may be practiced refer to diligently practicing the elimination and severance of these three kinds of unwholesome dharmas, whereby unwholesome dharmas are diminished and wholesome dharmas increase.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; I have now understood this meaning from the Buddha.”
If one further practices these three kinds of dharmas—doubt, longing, and idle speech—they will damage all wholesome dharmas and increase unwholesome ones.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu diligently practices to eliminate these three dharmas, he will attain the diminution of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome dharmas.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If there is a bhikṣu who practices the dharma of extinguishing falsehoods, how many kinds of bodies does he have?
The Buddha said,
“Lord of Devas!”
If there is a bhikṣu who practices the dharma of extinguishing falsehood, there are three kinds of bodies.
These three kinds of bodies are: the body of pleasure, the body of suffering, and the body of equanimity.
Regarding that which gladdens the body, there are two meanings: namely, that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.
That which is to be practiced refers to all wholesome dharmas;
that which is not to be practiced refers to all unwholesome dharmas.
"The body of suffering and the relinquishing of the body are likewise thus.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

So it is, so it is. Having now understood this meaning from the Buddha, I see that if a bhikṣu practices the dharma of the cessation of falsehood, then regarding the body of pleasure, the body of pain, and the body of equanimity—within these three types of bodies—all wholesome dharmas are to be practiced, while all unwholesome dharmas are not to be practiced.
At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Do all sentient beings have identical desires, recollections, and physical appearances?"
The Buddha said, “No,
Lord of Devas. All sentient beings do not have the same desires, the same thoughts, or the same physical appearances.”
"Lord of Devas!

Although all sentient beings each dwell within their respective realms and destinies, they are likewise unaware of the distinctions between those realms and destinies. Because they do not know these distinctions, they travel upon the path of darkness and, conversely, grasp at deluded phenomena as being real."

These sentient beings do not know the various distinctions between the realms and destinies; that which they perceive is only the realm of darkness. Although they perceive it, they constantly travel upon the path of darkness, firmly clinging to deluded phenomena as being real.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is so, it is so, just as the Buddha has taught. I now understand this meaning from the Buddha: all sentient beings do not have the same desires, do not have the same thoughts, and do not have the same physical forms. Because those sentient beings do not know these distinctions, they cling to the darkness of delusion as being real.”
At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others attain ultimate purity in the holy life?”
The Buddha said: "No. This has two meanings."
"Lord of Devas!
If those śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others cannot exhaust that dharma of craving, they will certainly not attain ultimate, pure brahmacarya."

If those śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others are able to exhaust that dharma of craving, they will attain unsurpassed liberation and the right liberation of mind; this is called attaining the ultimate purity of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is just as the Buddha has taught. I have now understood this meaning from the Buddha.”
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others do not exhaust the dharma of craving, they will certainly not attain ultimate, pure brahmacarya.

If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others who exhaust that dharma of craving, they will certainly attain unsurpassed liberation and the right liberation of mind; this is called attaining ultimate, pure brahmacarya.
At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How may I now forever leave behind the disease of all views so that they do not arise again?”
These various views and afflictions arise from the mind-consciousness; what then shall become of this mind-consciousness of mine?
Although I have questioned the Buddha on various matters, why am I unable to attain the fruit of sainthood and achieve the state of a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, and a Samyaksaṃbuddha?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will sever for me the root of doubt and the disease of all views.
The Buddha said,
"Lord of Devas!"
"Do you know this? In times past, there were śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who also asked about this same matter. Śakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I now recall that at one time, there were devas of great power gathered for the assembly of the Good Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, among those in the assembly, there were certain devas who, not knowing the Dharma, desired to become Buddhas on their own accord. With such an intention, they addressed the World-Honored One; the Buddha, perceiving their foolishness and ignorance, did not grant them a prediction.”

At that time, those devas, their wishes unfulfilled and their minds filled with dissatisfaction, rose from their seats and each returned to his own realm; yet as they did so, their realms no longer appeared, and they consequently fell away.
At that time, because they were about to fall, those devas were seized with great terror and doubt arose in their minds. Each of them thought:
"Since our original realm no longer appears, we certainly know we are falling. If we can find a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, we shall go to him and ask:
'Are you a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha?'"
At that time, some of those gods, seeing me walking alone in meditation, came to where I was and asked me:
"Virtuous one! Who are you?"
I then replied, "This is Śakra, the Lord of Devas. At that time,
because their hearts were filled with suffering and distress, those gods said:
"O Lord of Devas!

Do you not see that I am suffering in affliction? Because I failed to inquire about the Dharma from the Buddha when I ought to have done so, and failed to take refuge when I should have taken refuge, I returned to my own realm with a distracted mind; since my original realm no longer appears before me, I know for certain that I shall fall."
Therefore, being afflicted by suffering, I pray for your protection and deliverance.
O Lord of Devas!
From this day forth, I vow to take refuge in the Buddha as a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
At that time, I spoke these verses in reply to those devas:
"You have given rise to false thoughts, And what you say is not upright.
Seeking distinctions within the Buddha-mind, Because of this, you shall long suffer."
Whenever he saw a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa walking in meditation, he would immediately inquire: "Are you one who has attained perfect awakening?
If you are one who has attained perfect awakening, I shall take refuge in you and make offerings."
I then questioned him: "How should one make offerings?
He was unable to know what I asked regarding the Buddha’s true and right path.
At that time, the assembly of devas [disclosed] the inclinations of their hearts.
The mind and its mental factors are distinguished through doubt;
I know those mental phenomena as the World-Honored One has taught them.
Having understood them, I shall now explain them for you within these three realms.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the Great Teacher of the world.
Having successfully subdued the great army of Māra, he is able to deliver all sentient beings to the further shore of Nirvāṇa.
In the realms of gods and humans, there is none who can equal you;
O fearless Great Being, you have skillfully severed the disease of craving.
To the Tathāgata, the Honored One Vairocana, I now prostrate and pay homage.
At that time, after Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these words, the Buddha further addressed him, saying:
"Lord of Devas!
You may know those past matters, namely, the benefit of discernment and the benefit of gratification."
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now recall that once in the past, when the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated and retreated."
I had this thought: "Whatever happiness belongs to devas and humans, and whatever happiness belongs to asuras, I alone shall now enjoy and experience that delight.

Because of obtaining such an advantage of delight, throughout this entire life there will be strife and mutual injury with weapons; this is called the disadvantage resulting from that advantage of delight.

As for the benefit of discernment: throughout this single lifetime, there will be no strife or contention, even to the point that weapons and arms will not be used to harm one another; this is the benefit of discernment.
Śakra spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

Having now heard this true Dharma from the Buddha, my deep faith has increased further and I have resolved to cultivate vows and practices. I pray that when my life ends and I am reborn among humans, I shall be born into a wealthy and noble clan with vast stores of wealth and grain; that I may possess abundant treasures, palanquins, carriages, and articles of enjoyment; and that my retinue be flourishing and complete in every way, never lacking anything.”

May I be born into such a noble lineage and enter the womb of a wise mother; may my limbs be complete, my physical appearance exquisite, my food of the finest flavors, my status honorable and sovereign, and my lifespan long.

Having conceived right faith, they went forth from home toward the Buddha; shaving off their hair and beards and donning the dharma-robes, they became bhikṣus. Constantly maintaining the pure conduct (brahmacarya) without any transgression, they realized the fruits of srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin, even attaining the ultimate limit of the end of suffering.
“World-Honored One!
I have further heard that there is the Ultimate Heaven of Form (Ārūpyadhātu). I pray that at the end of my life in the human realm, I may be reborn in that heaven.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Lord of Devas!
Lord of Devas!”
"It shall be as you wish.
By what cause and by what condition has this sublime fruit of realization been attained? Śakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have no other cause; it is by hearing the True Dharma from the Buddha that I have given rise to profound faith, and through the power of my vows, I have realized such a fruit.”
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard the True Dharma within this assembly, by the power of that Dharma, my wisdom has increased and my lifespan has likewise been extended.
At that time, having made this vow, Śakra was distanced from and freed of dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, eighty thousand devas and humans also attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard the Dharma and seen the Dharma, was able to understand it; he abided firmly in the Dharma and severed all doubts.
Having realized this, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have attained liberation!"
"I have attained liberation!
From this day forth, for the remainder of my life, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and uphold the precepts of an upāsaka.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, turned to the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha in the presence of the Buddha and said:

"You have now brought me great benefit and merit, as well as profit to many people. Because you previously made offerings of such sublime joy to the Buddha, we have been able to hear the Dharma and attain its fruits. Wait until I have returned to my palace, and I shall fulfill your wish."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should produce the Brahma-voice and take the three refuges in the Buddha."
"What do you think?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has now attained the Brahma-abodes, tranquility, and Nirvana.

At that time, the assembly of devas followed Śakra around the Buddha three times, then prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, stood before him, and with one voice in a Brahma-like tone, took the Three Refuges in the Buddha, saying:

"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Having thus taken refuge in the Buddha three times, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his celestial host, as well as the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha and the others, vanished from the assembly and returned to their heavenly realm.

At that time, after the sun had passed and it was the middle of the night, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, came to where the Buddha was; his bodily radiance shone brilliantly, illuminating the Śakrasya Cave.
Having arrived before the Buddha, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke this verse:
“Śakra, for the sake of great benefit, Questioned the Buddha regarding the True Dharma;
The Buddha, with his subtle and wondrous voice, Has severed and eliminated all doubts.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Brahma King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is the time for the Buddha to preach the True Dharma."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; eighty thousand devas and humans likewise attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is."

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard the Buddha’s words, received them with joy and faith; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, vanished from sight, and returned to his celestial realm.
At that time, during the night, the World-Honored One went to where he sat surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"After this day had passed, during the night, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, came to where I was."
Having prostrated at my feet, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these verses:
“Śakra, for the sake of great benefit, Questioned the Buddha regarding the True Dharma;
The Buddha, with his subtle and wondrous voice, Has severed and eliminated all doubts.”
"Furthermore, he said to me:
'When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard the true Dharma, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and eighty thousand devas and humans likewise attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.'"
I then replied: "So it is, so it is.
At that time, having heard what I said, the Brahmā King rejoiced and accepted it with faith; he prostrated at my feet, vanished from sight, and returned to his celestial realm.
At that time, having heard the Buddha preach this Dharma, the assembly of bhikṣus were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
This concludes the *Sūtra on the Questions of Śakra* spoken by the Buddha.
